headline: 60 years
body: Every decade thought it had the answer.
punch: The current answer is only about 20 years old.

body: James Tanner proposed that growth slows because a central nervous system mechanism monitors body size and adjusts growth to follow a programmed trajectory.
punch: Sounded right for 40 years. Turned out to be the wrong organ.

body: Parfitt publishes a piece arguing the standard causal direction is inverted. Growth stops first because proliferative capacity runs out, and fusion follows as a consequence.
punch: A perspective piece. No experiment yet.

body: Nilsson and Baron transplant growth plates between animals of different ages. Growth rate follows the donor, never the recipient. The clock is inside the plate, not the body.
Continuous labelling in rabbits shows resting zone proliferation collapsing from over 95% at birth to under 10% by 17 weeks, with cell number dropping too.
punch: Now there's a number on the thing that runs out.

body: Estrogen turns out to do two separate things. Suppress growth rate, which reverses. And structurally deplete the progenitor pool, which doesn't.
punch: The most useful distinction in the field, and barely anyone repeats it.

body: A Hedgehog agonist bead in one rat femur produces measurable extra length against the untreated leg on the same animal.
punch: First direct evidence the reserve can be driven harder.

body: Single cell sequencing of human pubertal growth plate biopsies confirms the same stem cell populations exist in people, and that GH acts on them directly.
punch: Sixty years to get from a guess to human tissue.

headline: And right now
body: Nobody has established how fusion actually executes at the cellular level in humans. That's the live edge of the field today.
punch: Whatever replaces this timeline hasn't been written yet.
